title: simbasjungles/free-my-tv
author: simbasjungles
body:
# Free My TV **A fast, ad-free home screen for Google TV, LG and Samsung TVs.** Trending picks from your own apps, the weather at a glance, and a look that follows the sunset.
Open source. Built with Claude Code. One button to undo. [**freemytv.io**](https://freemytv.io) · [Install](#install) · [LG TVs](#lg-tvs-webos) · [Samsung TVs](#samsung-tvs-tizen) · [Any TV](#any-tv) · [Make it yours](#make-it-yours)
## What you get - **No ads.** No sponsored rows, banners or autoplaying promos. Not one. - **Your apps, front and center.** The streaming apps you actually use, on a glass shelf. Pick them and their order right on the TV. - **Trending, not sponsored.** Three fresh picks every hour (up to six, in Home Settings) from what's trending this week and the latest releases, only from apps you already have. Movies and Shows get their own tabs. - **Weather and markets, one press away.** The hour-by-hour forecast (or the next 5 days), sunrise and sunset, and live crypto prices. - **What's playing.** Music, a podcast or the radio going on in the background shows on the home screen and the screensaver: the title, the artist and the app, from any app that tells Android what it plays (*Home Settings*, off until you turn it on). - **Light by day, dark by night.** It follows your city's real sunset, the way your phone does. - **A screensaver to match.** Full-screen photos of the picks with a big glass clock. Optionally (*Watch from the screensaver*, in Home Settings), OK opens the title on screen in its app, and any other button just closes it. - **Your own photos** (Google TV and Android TV). Send them from your computer (up to 100): the screensaver shows them, and without picks one is the home screen's background each hour. - **Fast.** 60 fps, every frame in 16.6 ms, on the TV's own chip. The home screen uses 96 MB of memory instead of 242 MB (−60%).
Measured on a 98″ TCL Google TV running Android 14. - **Set up on the TV.** Language, your city, temperature, theme, how many picks and which streaming services they come from, the weather and prices cards, the forecast's hours or days, which coins, and the apps on the shelf, in Free My TV's own settings. - **Safe.** No root. Nothing is uninstalled. One button brings back the factory home screen. ## Install About ten minutes. You need a Google TV or Android TV (Android 8 or newer) and a computer on the same Wi-Fi. ### The easy way: an AI assistant 1. **On the TV**, turn on developer mode: Settings → System → About → press *Android TV OS build* 7 times. Then Settings → System → Developer options → turn on **USB debugging**. Write down the TV's IP address (Settings → Network & Internet). 2. **On your computer**, open an AI coding assistant ([Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code), Codex or Antigravity) and say: > Install Free My TV (github.com/simbasjungles/free-my-tv) on my TV at 192.168.1.50. I live in Lisbon. It downloads the code, installs the tools it needs, builds the app and puts it on your TV, and asks before anything important. Swap in your TV's IP and your city. 3. **On the TV**, open *Free My TV* → *Home Screen* → *Free My TV*. That's when the TV asks *Allow USB debugging?* for Free My TV: tick *Always allow* and accept. ### The ready APK No tools to install besides adb. The APK on the [latest release](https://github.com/simbasjungles/free-my-tv/releases/latest) has no TMDB key: add yours on the TV for the picks (*Home Settings* → *TMDB key*, [below](#the-tmdb-key)). It takes your city from the TV's time zone (change it in *Home Settings* → *City*). 1. **On the TV**, do step 1 above. 2. **On your computer**, download `FreeMyTV.apk` from the release and install it: ```bash adb connect 192.168.1.50:5555 adb install -r FreeMyTV.apk ``` On Android 14, Google Play Protect may hold the install with *Risky app blocked*: choose *More details* → *Install anyway*. 3. **On the TV**, do step 3 above. If you built Free My TV yourself before, switch back to *Original* and uninstall it first: your build and the release are signed with different keys. For the picks, add your TMDB key in *Home Settings* → *TMDB key* (below). **Updates come to the TV.** Once a week the APK from the release looks for a newer release and downloads it; the home screen then says so once, and *Home Settings* → *Updates* (the last row) installs it through Android's installer, which asks first (and, the first time, asks to allow Free My TV to install apps). OK on *Updates* also checks right away. The download must come from this repository's releases, match the size and SHA-256 GitHub lists, be newer, and be signed with the project's key. A build you made yourself checks only when you press *Updates*, and only says when a new version is out: build it again to update. ### The manual way 1. **On the TV**, do step 1 above. 2. **Tools:** a JDK (17+), the Android SDK command-line tools (build-tools 34, platform android-34) and adb. On a Mac: ```bash brew install --cask temurin android-commandlinetools android-platform-tools sdkmanager "build-tools;34.0.0" "platforms;android-34" ``` On Linux, get OpenJDK 17, Android's command-line tools and adb from your package manager, then run the same `sdkmanager` line. On Windows, use Git Bash (which Claude Code uses there) or WSL. 3. **Build:** ```bash ./build.sh ``` The first run creates `config.properties`. Set your city and your [TMDB key](#the-tmdb-key) there, then run it again. 4. **Install:** ```bash adb connect 192.168.1.50:5555 adb install -r FreeMyTV.apk ``` If the install seems stuck, look at the TV: on Android 14, Google Play Protect may hold it with *Risky app blocked* ("built for an older version of Android"), since Free My TV targets Android 13. Choose *More details* → *Install anyway*. Updates don't ask again. Chromecast with Google TV on Android 14 keeps port 5555 closed even with USB debugging on: turn on *Wireless debugging* (Developer options), pair with `adb pair `, then run `adb tcpip 5555` over that connection. Port 5555 closes again at every restart, so after one, *Original*, the watchdog and the boot check can't reach ADB until you run `adb tcpip 5555` again (the pairing stays). On TCL TVs, also let it run in the background (TCL blocks it by default, and the switch never starts): ```bash adb shell "appops set io.freemytv AUTO_START allow || appops set io.freemytv APP_AUTO_START allow" ``` 5. **On the TV**, open *Free My TV* → *Home Screen* → *Free My TV*. The TV asks *Allow USB debugging?* once more, now for Free My TV itself: tick *Always allow* and accept. (Run `adb disconnect 192.168.1.50:5555` first: on Android 8 to 10 the TV can hand that answer to a computer that's still connected.) On some TCL TVs (Android 11, Realtek), a second background killer, TGuard, can stop the switch while it measures the original home screen: the settings screen closes and the TV's own home screen stays. Android runs the switch again by itself within a minute or two; then press Home: Free My TV opening means it went through. ## LG TVs (webOS) The same home screen as an LG app: the picks, the glass shelf with your apps, the drawer with inputs, weather and prices, day and night, Home Settings and the shelf editor. It installs through LG's own Developer Mode, with nothing rooted or changed on the TV. LG's home screen stays where it is, and Free My TV is one press of a number key away (or in LG's app list, on remotes without them). You need an LG TV (webOS 3 or newer) and a computer on the same Wi-Fi, with Python 3. 1. **On the TV**, open the LG Content Store and install **Developer Mode**. Sign in with a free [LG developer account](https://webostv.developer.lge.com), turn on **Dev Mode Status** (the TV restarts), then turn on **Key Server**. Write down the IP address and the passphrase it shows. 2. **On your computer**, get the code and build. `config.properties` works as for Google TV (your city, your [TMDB key](#the-tmdb-key)): ```bash git clone https://github.com/simbasjungles/free-my-tv && cd free-my-tv python3 webos/build.py ``` 3. **Install.** The first time, it asks for the TV's passphrase; updates don't: ```bash python3 webos/install.py 192.168.1.50 ``` 4. **On the TV**, while Free My TV is open, hold a number key on the remote. From then on, that key opens it from anywhere. On a remote without number keys, open it from LG's app list on the home screen, like any other app. With an AI assistant, say *"Install Free My TV (github.com/simbasjungles/free-my-tv) on my LG TV at 192.168.1.50. I live in Lisbon."* It builds the app and hands you the install command, so you type the passphrase yourself. With the [webOS Homebrew Channel](https://github.com/webosbrew/webos-homebrew-channel), you can skip the computer: add the repository `https://freemytv.io/webos/apps.json` in the Channel's settings, and Free My TV shows up in its list. That's the release build: it takes the city from the TV's time zone (change it in *Home Settings* → *City*), and for the picks you type your [TMDB key](#the-tmdb-key) in *Home Settings* → *TMDB key*. If you installed your own build, don't update it from there, or the release replaces it. On webOS 6 and newer, LG doesn't let apps installed through Developer Mode see which apps the TV has. Free My TV then shows the well-known ones it finds (Netflix, YouTube, Prime Video, Disney+, Apple TV, Plex and more) and asks the TV, once, for the access LG's phone app uses: a message on the TV asks whether to allow Free My TV. Allow it, and from the next start all your apps show, with their icons. Older LG TVs (webOS 3) don't let Free My TV see their apps at all, so the shelf stays empty. There your computer asks the TV instead (the TV asks once whether to allow it), and the list and icons are built into the app. Run it again after installing new apps on the TV: ```bash python3 webos/apps.py 192.168.1.50 && python3 webos/build.py && python3 webos/install.py 192.168.1.50 ``` Developer Mode lasts about 40 days: open the Developer Mode app now and then and press **EXTEND**. To remove Free My TV, run `python3 webos/install.py 192.168.1.50 --uninstall`. ## Samsung TVs (Tizen) The same home screen as a Samsung app, with everything the LG one has: the picks, the shelf, the drawer with the inputs, the weather and the prices, day and night, and its own settings. It installs through Samsung's own Developer Mode, with nothing rooted or changed on the TV, and Samsung's home screen stays where it is. You need a Samsung TV on Tizen, from 2015 or newer, and a computer on the same Wi-Fi (a 2015 UE48JU6100 on Tizen 2.3 was reported working, #317; Orsay models can't run it, but a Google TV streamer on HDMI can). 2015 and 2016 TVs can't run TizenBrew, so on those build it yourself (below); TV Settings isn't in the drawer there, since apps can't open the TV's settings. 1. **On the TV**, open **Apps** and type `1 2 3 4 5` on the remote. Turn **Developer mode** on, type your computer's IP address in **Host PC IP**, and restart the TV. 2. **On your computer**, download [TizenBrew Installer](https://github.com/reisxd/TizenBrewInstaller/releases/latest), the community's installer for Samsung TVs, open it and connect to your TV. 3. **Install from GitHub:** type `simbasjungles/free-my-tv`. On 2023 and newer TVs it asks you to sign in to your Samsung account once, to sign the app for your TV. 4. **Straight to it:** in the TV's settings, under Start Screen Options, turn on **Autorun Last App**: the TV turns on into Free My TV. This build takes your city from the TV's time zone (change it in *Home Settings* → *City*), and for the trending picks you type your [TMDB key](#the-tmdb-key) in *Home Settings* → *TMDB key*. To build it with your own `config.properties` instead, open the folder in Claude Code and say *"Install Free My TV on my Samsung TV at 192.168.1.50. I live in Lisbon."* It sets up Samsung's tools, and on 2023 and newer TVs you sign in to your Samsung account in the browser to make the certificate. Your signed build installs with `python3 tizen/install.py 192.168.1.50`, which needs only Python: no Tizen Studio, and no Rosetta on Apple Silicon Macs. ## Settings The first values come from `config.properties`, created by the first build (Google TV, LG and Samsung use the same file). Most of them can also be changed on the TV, in *Free My TV* → *Home Settings*, and the TV's choice wins: | Key | What it does | Default | |---|---|---| | `tmdb_key` | Your free TMDB key, for the picks | empty | | `tmdb_region` | Your country (two letters): which titles are on which app | `US` | | `watchmode_key` | Optional, free [Watchmode](https://api.watchmode.com/) key: a pick opens the title's page in its app | empty | | `plex_url` and `plex_token` | Optional, your Plex server's `plex.direct` address and token: its newest titles join the picks and open on their page | empty | | `latitude`, `longitude` | Your city, for the weather and the sunset | New York | | `city` | The name on the weather card | `Weather` | | `hide_animation` | Leave cartoons and anime out of the picks | `false` | | `language` | `auto` (follows the TV), or a language with a [translation](#translations) (`en`, `pt`, `es`, `de`, `ru`, `fr`, `ja`…) | `auto` | | `show_crypto` | Show Binance crypto prices on home and screensaver | `true` | | `currency` | Crypto prices in `USD`, `EUR`, `BRL`… | `USD` | | `temperature` | `C`, `F` or `auto` | `auto` | | `theme` | `auto` (dark from sunset to sunrise), `light` or `dark` | `auto` | | `disable_assistant` | Also turn off Google Assistant | `false` | | `screensaver` | `false` keeps the TV's own screensaver: Free My TV then changes only the home screen and the promo apps (Google TV) | `true` | | `hide_services` | Streaming services to leave out of the picks even when their app is on the TV (`netflix`, `prime`, `disney`…), comma separated; for apps the TV ships that you don't subscribe to. It is where the switches in Home Settings › Picks › Picks from start; what you switch on the TV wins. Google TV only | empty | | `hide_apps` | Apps to leave out of the shelf, All Apps and the picks, by id or name (part of it), comma separated; for apps the TV ships that can't be uninstalled, like Samsung's built-in Netflix. LG and Samsung only | empty | | `shelf_apps` | The shelf's apps in this order, by id or name (part of it), comma separated; changing it wins once over the shelf picked on the TV. On Samsung, a whole app id also brings an app the TV leaves out of its list, like one installed in Developer Mode. LG and Samsung only | empty | | `drawer_first` | `true` opens the home screen with the drawer already out (apps in the middle, inputs, weather and prices below), so nothing has to be scrolled to reach the inputs; Back closes it to the full page. For a TV whose streaming apps live on a box, where the picks stay empty. LG and Samsung only | `false` | Changed something? Run `./build.sh` and install again. Keep `freemytv.keystore`: updates are signed with it. ### The TMDB key Free, and it takes two minutes: create an account at [themoviedb.org](https://www.themoviedb.org/signup), then open [Settings → API](https://www.themoviedb.org/settings/api) and request a developer key. Paste the *API Read Access Token* (or the *API Key*) after `tmdb_key=`. It's your key: `config.properties` stays out of git. On Google TV and Android TV you can also add it on the TV, which the APK from the releases needs: *Home Settings* → *TMDB key* shows a QR code. Scan it with your phone (on the same Wi-Fi), paste the key and send it; the TV checks it with TMDB and keeps it. The code works once, for 5 minutes, and only while it's on screen. The phone's page is plain HTTP on your own Wi-Fi: on a network you don't trust (a hotel's), type the key instead. No phone at hand? *Type it with the remote*: the short *API Key* (32 characters) is the easier one to type. A key added on the TV wins over the one in `config.properties`, and *Remove the key* goes back to it. On LG and Samsung you can also type it on the TV, in *Home Settings* → *TMDB key*: the short *API Key* (32 characters) is the easier one to type with the remote. TMDB checks it before it's saved, it stays on the TV, and it wins over the one in `config.properties` (*Remove the key* goes back to that one). ### Opening a title, not just its app (optional) With a free [Watchmode](https://api.watchmode.com/) key (`watchmode_key=` in `config.properties`), a pick opens its own page in the streaming app instead of the app's home. The free plan (2,500 credits a month) is enough: each title costs two requests the first time and is remembered after that. It works where the app takes the title's web address (tested: Prime Video and JioHotstar); where it doesn't, the pick just opens the app, as without a key. ### Your own photos (optional) On Google TV and Android TV, with the TV connected over adb (see *Install*), send photos or whole folders from your computer: ```bash python3 tools/photos.py beach.jpg hills.jpg Holidays/ ``` They land in the app's own folder on the TV (no permission needed); on Android 11, which keeps adb out of other apps' folders, they go through Free My TV itself. The next time the home screen, the screensaver or Free My TV's settings open, the app imports each one: turned upright, cropped to 16:9, resized for the TV and saved without its GPS and other tags; what was sent is then deleted. The screensaver shows them in the order you sent them, instead of the picks' photos; without a TMDB key, one of them is the home screen's background, a new one every hour. *Home Settings* → *My Photos*: the arrows turn them on or off, OK removes them. Up to 100; JPEG, PNG and WebP, and HEIC on Android 9 and newer. ### Your Plex library (optional) Set `plex_url` and `plex_token` in `config.properties`, and one of the newest movies and one of the newest shows of your Plex server (another one each time the list is made, a few times a day, among the latest 8 of each kind) join the picks, with their own poster and backdrop, tagged "Plex". A tab shows at most one. Selecting one opens the title's page in the Plex app. If the server can't be reached when the list is made, its titles are left out. This is for Google TV and Android TV, and it needs the TMDB key and at least one streaming app on the TV: without those no picks come at all, Plex included. - **`plex_url`** is the server's own `plex.direct` address, which has a valid certificate (the TV checks it as for any site; plain `http` and any other address are ignored, so a typo never sends your token anywhere). It looks like `https://192-168-1-20.0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef.plex.direct:32400`: your server's local IP with dashes, then its id. Open any item in Plex's web app, *Get Info → View XML*, and the address bar has it, before `/library/...`. - **`plex_token`** is on the same address, after `X-Plex-Token=`. It gives access to your Plex account, and any app on the TV can read the APK it is built into, so use the token of a Plex Home *managed user* with access to your libraries, not your own, and never commit it. The TV talks to your server directly on your network. If the server can't be reached, the other picks load as usual. ## Going back On the TV: *Free My TV* → *Home Screen* → *Original*. The factory home screen, screensaver and every app come back exactly as they were. If the new home screen ever crashes three times in five minutes, it switches back by itself. To remove it for good, switch to *Original* first, then uninstall *Free My TV* (Settings → Apps). Uninstalled it while it was on? Install it again and pick *Original*: the list of what it turned off is kept in the TV's settings, so everything comes back. ## What it changes - It becomes the home screen and, unless `screensaver=false`, the screensaver. - It turns off, without uninstalling: - the stock home screen and screensaver (the screensaver stays with `screensaver=false`); - Google TV's recovery home, Play Games and YouTube Music; - on TCL TVs, the TCL Channel, messages, store demo, hotel menu, manuals, mirroring and logging apps; - on Philco TVs, AI PONT (promo channels and app downloads) and the manual; - on Multilaser TVs, Anoki's screen-content recognition (ACR), the store demo and the manual; - on KTC-made TVs (NextStar), Anoki's screen-content recognition (ACR), the store demo and the manual; - Google Assistant, only with `disable_assistant=true`. - On Google TV, the Assistant's results for films and shows come from Google TV's home app, which is off in Free My TV mode: asking it to play a show can end in "Sorry, I don't understand", and a search can show only YouTube videos. Opening apps, questions and apps' own voice search (YouTube's, for one) still work; *Original* brings it all back. - On TCL TVs, the remote's Netflix, YouTube and Prime buttons keep working through a small accessibility service that only reads those buttons. Pick what each one opens in *Free My TV* → *Remote Buttons*; *Original* turns the service off. On TCL TVs with Android 11 the service stays off, since with it the TV moved the volume two steps per press: there the buttons work on Free My TV's home screen. On Vestel-made TVs (F&U and other store brands) and Xiaomi (Formovie) projectors the same goes for the Netflix button, and on KTC-made TVs (NextStar) for the Tabii button. On Sony TVs, the BRAVIA CORE, Netflix, Disney+, Prime Video, YouTube and Crunchyroll buttons (and Google Play, on remotes that have it) can each open the app you pick, or keep Sony's default. On Xiaomi TVs whose remote has a Mi button instead of Home, that button opens Free My TV instead of PatchWall (or, if you pick it, PatchWall as before, or another app). On Xiaomi TVs, the YouTube button opens YouTube again (Google TV's home screen answered it), and the PatchWall button can open the app you pick. On Xiaomi TVs sold in Russia, the same goes for the Okko, VK, Rutube, KION, Wink and IVI buttons, which keep Xiaomi's default until you pick another app. On Hisense TVs, the Prime Video, YouTube, Disney+, All Apps, Settings and profile buttons, which Google TV's home screen answered, open what you pick (All Apps opens Free My TV's own; Netflix stays with the TV). On any of these TVs, setting every button to *Nothing* (or the brand's default) turns the service off. - With *Home Settings* → *Now Playing widget* on (it starts off), what an app is playing shows in place of the prices while it plays, on the home screen and the screensaver. Android hands that only to a notification listener, so turning the widget on allows ours through the TV's ADB; turning it off, *Original* and the switch back after crashes take it away. Where the TV refuses it, the row says so. - On HY300 projectors, whose stock home screen was the only way to them, the bottom drawer gets *Keystone* (keystone, zoom and projection mode) and *Screen Mirroring* (the projector's Miracast receiver), and HDMI opens through the projector's own player. - *Free My TV* → *Sleep Timer* turns the TV off after 5 minutes to 4 hours, with the minutes left over any app (top center, or the corner you pick). It presses the remote's Sleep key through the TV's own ADB, so it works in Free My TV mode; *Original* stops it. - Picture, sound, inputs, remote pairing, Google services and the Play Store are on a protected list, checked before every change, and so are Android's own pieces and factory menus. Before anything goes off, the TV is asked whether its inputs or its remote's Input key depend on it; those stay on. - On Google TV, the setup app goes off before the stock home screen and comes back after it, so its recovery screen never takes over the Home button in between. - Apps that saved a Wi-Fi network are never turned off, since Android would erase the network. If the TV's first setup saved yours, the switch asks you to forget the network and connect again in Settings first (saved networks out of range don't show there; Claude Code can remove them). ## Any TV Free My TV runs on Google TV and Android TV: TCL, Sony, Hisense, Philips, Xiaomi, Vestel-made TVs (F&U), KTC-made TVs (NextStar) and more, plus streamers like Chromecast with Google TV, the Google TV Streamer, onn 4K, the Xiaomi Mi TV Stick and NVIDIA Shield, and projectors like the Wanbo T2 Ultra. And on [LG](#lg-tvs-webos) and [Samsung](#samsung-tvs-tizen) TVs, as an app. **Any other TV:** plug a Google TV streamer into HDMI and free that one. Same steps, same home screen. **A different brand or model:** ask Claude. Free My TV is made to be adapted by AI. Open the folder in Claude Code and say *"set it up for my Sony"*: it reads your TV, finds its home screen and its promo apps, updates the lists below and walks you through a test. [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) tells it how. | What | Where | |---|---| | Apps to turn off | `DEBLOAT` in [`HomeMode.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeMode.java) | | Apps never to touch | `PROTECTED` in the same file | | Apps on the shelf | `SHELF` in [`HomeApps.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeApps.java) | | Your brand's live TV app | `LIVE_TV_APPS` in the same file | ## Make it yours It's your code, and Claude Code finds its way around it. Try: - *"Add Crunchyroll to the shelf."* - *"Show the prices in euros."* - *"Add Catalan."* - *"Switch to the night look an hour after sunset."* ## How it works - **A plain Android app, no Gradle, no libraries.** [`build.sh`](build.sh) runs aapt2 → javac → d8 → zipalign → apksigner and makes a 2 MB APK. - **It uses the TV's own ADB, from inside the TV.** The app connects to `127.0.0.1:5555` with its own key (that's the *Allow USB debugging?* prompt) and runs the same commands you would: `cmd package set-home-activity`, `settings put secure screensaver_components`, `pm disable-user`. Nothing listens to the network. - **Drawn by hand on one Canvas**, with Android 13 shaders for the frosted glass and the sky (plain fills on Android 8 to 12, with lighter shadows and no GPU layers on 8 to 11 for their older GPUs). - **A safety net.** A watchdog in a separate process brings back the stock home screen after three crashes in five minutes, and a boot check keeps your choice after TV updates. - **On LG and Samsung, the same design in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript** ([`web/`](web)), written for the Chromium of older TVs, with no frameworks. [`webos/build.py`](webos/build.py) packs it with `config.properties` into an `.ipk` without LG's tools, and [`webos/install.py`](webos/install.py) installs it through Developer Mode; on LG it lists and opens apps through the TV's own service bus (Luna), as LG's launcher does. [`tizen/build.py`](tizen/build.py) packs the same app into a Samsung `.wgt`, which uses Tizen's web APIs for the apps and the inputs. To preview it on a computer: `python3 webos/build.py --preview`, then open `out/webos/index.html` (a stand-in lists sample apps). - **Data** from TMDB (trending titles, new releases and which app streams what in your country), Open-Meteo (forecast, sunrise and sunset), and optionally Binance (24-hour prices when `show_crypto=true`). | File | What it is | |---|---| | [`HomeView.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeView.java) | The home screen | | [`HomeMode.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeMode.java) | Switching between Free My TV and Original | | [`Adb.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/Adb.java) | The TV's own ADB, from inside the TV | | [`Recs.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/Recs.java) | The picks (TMDB) | | [`KeyPage.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/KeyPage.java), [`Qr.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/Qr.java) | The TMDB key sent from a phone, and its QR code | | [`HomeData.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeData.java) | Weather and prices | | [`HomeApps.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/HomeApps.java) | The shelf, inputs and All Apps | | [`DreamView.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/DreamView.java) | The screensaver | | [`SettingsActivity.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/SettingsActivity.java) | The settings screen (the app's icon) | | [`Prefs.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/Prefs.java) | Settings changed on the TV | | [`RemoteKeys.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/RemoteKeys.java) | The remote's app buttons (TCL, Sony, Xiaomi and others) | | [`Watchdog.java`](app/src/io/freemytv/Watchdog.java) | The safety net | | [`web/home.js`](web/home.js) | The home screen on LG TVs | | [`web/tv.js`](web/tv.js) | The TV's apps and inputs, on LG and Samsung | | [`webos/build.py`](webos/build.py), [`webos/install.py`](webos/install.py) | The LG app package and its install | | [`tizen/build.py`](tizen/build.py) | The Samsung app package | The website ([freemytv.io](https://freemytv.io)) is in [`docs/`](docs): plain HTML, CSS and JS on GitHub Pages. ## Translations On Google TV, LG and Samsung, each language is one file, [`app/assets/i18n/.json`](app/assets/i18n), keyed by the English text in the code. *Automatic* follows the TV's language and uses any language that has a file (English otherwise); *Home Settings* → *Language* lists them all. Today: English, Portuguese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Dutch, Polish, Swedish, Danish, Norwegian, Finnish, Czech, Romanian, Turkish, Russian, Ukrainian, Greek, Japanese, Korean, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, Hindi, Indonesian, Vietnamese and Thai. Portuguese, Spanish, German, Russian, Thai and Turkish were translated by hand and are the reference (fix them by hand); the others were machine-made, and corrections from native speakers are welcome. - **Add a language:** `python3 tools/translate.py --new ca`, then fill `app/assets/i18n/ca.json` by hand, or with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` set, `python3 tools/translate.py --fill --lang ca` (only the strings go to the API). - **After changing text in the code:** `python3 tools/translate.py` lists what each language lacks; `--fill` translates only that (the hand-translated ones, Portuguese, Spanish, German, Russian, Thai and Turkish, are left for a person unless `--lang` names them), `--prune` drops strings the code no longer uses. Run `python3 tools/translate.py --check` to validate all catalogues without writing files. - Text built at runtime has placeholders (`"{n} min ago"`), so each language puts the words in its own order. A key like `"unit|Automatic"` is the same English in another place, where a language may need another word. - Counts have plural forms: `"plural|one:{n} season|other:{n} seasons"` is translated with one form per plural category the language uses (Russian `"one:{n} сезон|few:{n} сезона|many:{n} сезонов|other:{n} сезона"`, Japanese just `"other:{n}シーズン"`), and Android's plural rules pick the one for each number. - **Limits:** right-to-left languages (Arabic, Hebrew, Persian) would need the layout mirrored, so they aren't there yet. Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Hindi are drawn with the TV's system font (Inter has no such letters). ## Privacy No accounts, no analytics, no tracking. The app talks to TMDB, Open-Meteo (with the coordinates you set, or your time zone's main city), and Binance only when `show_crypto=true`, Watchmode only when you set a `watchmode_key`, and your Plex server only when you set a `plex_url`. On Google TV and Android TV, the APK from the release asks GitHub (api.github.com) once a week, or when you press *Updates*, for the latest release, and when there's a newer one downloads it from github.com and GitHub's download server (release-assets.githubusercontent.com); a build you made yourself asks only when you press *Updates*. The *Now Playing widget* reads what apps are playing (title, artist, the app) through a notification listener, the only way Android shares it: Free My TV allows the listener only while the widget is on, never reads a notification with it, and asks Android to unbind it as soon as it connects, so it stays unbound. What's playing never leaves the TV. While *Home Settings* → *TMDB key* shows its QR code (5 minutes at most), the TV answers on your home network at that code's address, for one key; the key goes to TMDB only, to check it. Your settings stay on your computer and your TV. ## Credits - Built with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code). - The LG version builds on what [@danielthejoker18](https://github.com/danielthejoker18) found in [FreeMyTvWebOS](https://github.com/danielthejoker18/FreeMyTvWebOS) (MIT): installing through Developer Mode and opening apps through the TV's service bus. - On Samsung TVs it installs with [TizenBrew Installer](https://github.com/reisxd/TizenBrewInstaller) by [@reisxd](https://github.com/reisxd). - This product uses the TMDB API but is not endorsed or certified by [TMDB](https://www.themoviedb.org/). - Links to the titles in the streaming apps by [Watchmode](https://api.watchmode.com/). - Weather data by [Open-Meteo.com](https://open-meteo.com/) (CC BY 4.0). Prices from the [Binance](https://www.binance.com/) public API. - Icons: [Material Symbols](https://fonts.google.com/icons) (Apache 2.0). Font: [Inter](https://rsms.me/inter/) (SIL OFL 1.1). Coin logos: [cryptocurrency-icons](https://github.com/spothq/cryptocurrency-icons) (CC0). Samsung app logos: [Simple Icons](https://simpleicons.org) (CC0). - The QR code encoder follows Project Nayuki's [QR Code generator](https://www.nayuki.io/page/qr-code-generator-library) (MIT). - Not affiliated with Google, TCL, LG, Samsung or any streaming service. App names and logos belong to their owners. ## License [MIT](LICENSE). Fork it, change it, ship it.

title: Jakeschincariol/replica-skill
author: Jakeschincariol
body:
# The Replica skill

Eleven Claude skills that clone any app. Free, MIT, no signup, no API key,
nothing to connect.

One reverse-engineers the app you want to clone. One rebuilds it. One tests it
for bugs. And one is the Entrepreneur: it reads what the app's users hate and
fixes it in yours, so you have an app you can sell.

In between, the others plan the stack and the database, rebuild the design
system, wire up auth and payments, score your clone against the original, give
it a name and a brand of its own, write the landing page and the store
listing, and put it live on your domain.

**It rebuilds what an app does, never what it owns.** Features and flows,
clean-room style. Not its code, its logo, its copy or its content. The
fine print is at the bottom, and the skills enforce it.

## Install

Paste this into Claude:

```
https://github.com/Jakeschincariol/replica-skill

install skill
```

Or as a plugin, in Claude Code:

```
/plugin marketplace add Jakeschincariol/replica-skill
/plugin install replica-skill@replica-skill
```

Claude Code namespaces plugin skills, so installed as a plugin they show up as
`/replica-skill:replica-recon` and so on. Copy the folders instead if you want
plain `/replica-recon`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Jakeschincariol/replica-skill.git
cp -r replica-skill/replica-* ~/.claude/skills/
```

Project-local instead of global: copy the same folders into your repo's
`.claude/skills/`. No Claude Code at all? Paste any single `SKILL.md` at the
top of a chat and it runs as a mode. You lose the Python tools, but the
method works.

The tools need Python 3.8 or newer. Nothing to pip install.

## The eleven

| command | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/replica-recon` | Reverse-engineers any app: screens, flows, components, data model. From public pages, screenshots, store listings and your own account. |
| `/replica-architect` | Plans the stack, database schema and API for your clone. |
| `/replica-design` | Rebuilds the design system: colours, type, spacing, components. As tokens, with your own assets. |
| `/replica-build` | Rebuilds the app screen by screen from the recon map. |
| `/replica-backend` | Auth, database, payments and integrations. |
| `/replica-test` | Clicks through every flow and tests it for bugs. |
| `/replica-diff` | Compares your clone against the original. A parity score and what is missing. |
| `/replica-entrepreneur` | Reads what the app's users hate in real reviews and turns it into fixes and a positioning angle. |
| `/replica-brand` | Names and rebrands your version so it is yours. |
| `/replica-launch` | Landing page, pricing and App Store listing. |
| `/replica-deploy` | Ships it live on your own domain. |

## How to use it

Run them in order. Each one reads what the last one wrote, in a `replica/`
folder in your project.

```
recon -> architect -> design -> build -> backend -> test -> diff -> entrepreneur -> brand -> launch -> deploy
```

An example: cloning a scheduling app, the kind where you share a link and
people book a time with you.

1. **`/replica-recon`** with the app's URL. It reads the help center, the
   pricing page, the store listing and public walkthroughs, and you click
   through your own account with it. Out comes `replica/recon.md`: 18
   screens, 7 flows (guest books a meeting, host sets availability, guest
   reschedules...), the components, an inferred data model (users, event
   types, availability, bookings) and `features.csv`. The partner
   marketplace is marked out of scope: that is their network, not a feature.
2. **`/replica-architect`** picks Next.js, Postgres, Stripe and Resend, writes
   the schema (with a constraint so two guests can never book the same slot)
   and orders the build: the booking flow end to end first.
3. **`/replica-design`** measures the screenshots into tokens: colour roles,
   type scale, 8px spacing, the date picker and slot button specs. Open
   icons, an open font, your own words.
4. **`/replica-build`** builds the shell, then the booking flow, then every
   screen with all its states, ticking off `features.csv` as it goes.
5. **`/replica-backend`** adds sign up, Google Calendar through Google's own
   API with your keys, Stripe for paid bookings, reminder emails.
6. **`/replica-test`** writes a test plan from the 7 flows, Playwright specs
   for the happy paths and edge cases (time zones, a slot taken mid-booking,
   double submit), and logs bugs by severity until no S1 or S2 is open.
7. **`/replica-diff`** scores it. Features 86, all must-haves done, booking
   page layout 91. Missing: round-robin for teams, the website embed.
8. **`/replica-entrepreneur`** reads 140 real reviews across the App Store,
   G2, Capterra and Reddit. Top complaints: per-seat price jumps, no text
   reminders, guests confused by time zones. Each with counts and linked
   quotes. Fix plan: flat pricing, SMS reminders, a time zone confirm step.
   Angle: booking links for small teams that hate per-seat pricing.
9. **`/replica-brand`** names it (with the trademark and domain checks to
   run), gives it a new palette, a logo brief and a voice, then sweeps the
   codebase until nothing of the original is left.
10. **`/replica-launch`** writes the landing page around the angle, sets
    pricing against the original's public page, and lints the store listing.
11. **`/replica-deploy`** runs the preflight (tests, parity, sweep, listing),
    sets up production, gives you the DNS records for your domain, and ships
    it when you say go.

You can also run any one on its own. `/replica-entrepreneur` on an app you
are only thinking about cloning is a good way to find out if you should.

## The tools

Six of them, all standard-library Python. None touch the network.

```bash
python3 replica-diff/imgdiff.py original.png clone.png --out diff.png   # layout diff, ignores colour
python3 replica-diff/parity.py replica/features.csv                     # parity score + missing list
python3 replica-entrepreneur/reviews.py replica/reviews.csv             # what users hate, ranked, linked
python3 replica-design/contrast.py replica/design/tokens.json           # WCAG contrast on your tokens
python3 replica-brand/sweep.py . --avoid "Original App"                 # anything of the original left?
python3 replica-launch/listing.py replica/launch/listing.json           # store limits + copycat checks
```

**`imgdiff.py`** reads PNGs with no libraries, turns both screenshots into
edge maps and compares where things are, so your new colours do not count
against you. It tells you which regions differ, in the original's pixels.

**`parity.py`** weights must, should and could, counts partial as half, and
never scores what you left out on purpose or what you added. Missing
must-haves means not shippable, and it says so.

**`reviews.py`** drops every review without a link. Every quote it prints is
copied from a row you gave it, with that row's URL. Themes with under three
reviews or one source are marked thin.

**`sweep.py`** finds the original's name, domain and colours anywhere in your
code, including inside identifiers like `OriginalAppEmbed`, and blocks the
deploy until it is clean.

**`listing.py`** checks App Store and Google Play limits, ranking claims in
the title, wasted keyword characters, and the original's name anywhere in
your listing.

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

## Fine print

**It rebuilds functionality and UX patterns, clean-room style.** It studies
what the app does and how people move through it, then writes everything
fresh. It never copies the target's source code, proprietary assets, logos,
trademarks, copy or private APIs.

**It only reads what you are allowed to read.** Public pages and your own
account. It never scrapes behind a login or against a site's terms, never
logs into anyone else's account, and never gets past a paywall. If your
account's terms forbid using it to build a competitor, it says so and sticks
to public sources.

**It always rebrands before launch.** New name, new palette, new logo, new
words. `/replica-deploy` will not ship until the sweep is clean.

**"Clone any app" means the features and the flow.** Not the content, the
network or the licences an app owns. You can rebuild a music app's player,
playlists and sharing. You cannot clone its catalogue.

**No guarantee of a "perfect" clone.** Results depend on how complex the app
is. A booking tool is weeks. A spreadsheet engine is not. `/replica-recon`
sizes it honestly before you start, and `/replica-diff` gives you a real
number, not a vibe.

**The Entrepreneur never makes things up.** No invented reviews, quotes or
numbers. Every claim has a link, and the sample size is stated.

**Check before you sell.** Run the trademark checks `/replica-brand` lists,
read the terms of anything you used, and talk to a lawyer before launch if
there is money on the line. This is not legal advice.

## Files

```
replica-recon/         SKILL.md, recon-map.md, features.csv (the matrix template)
replica-architect/     SKILL.md, architecture.md
replica-design/        SKILL.md, tokens.json, contrast.py
```

body:
Sassy

Welcome to **Sassy**, a powerful template generator designed to accelerate the development of Micro-SaaS applications. Built with **Next.js 15**, **TypeScript**, **TailwindCSS**, **Supabase**, and **Stripe**, Sassy provides a robust foundation for building subscription-based services with integrated authentication, subscription management, and payment processing. | **Feature** | **Status** | |-----------------------------------------|------------| | OAuth Authentication (Google, FB, Twitter) | ✅ | | Subscription & Billing (Stripe) | ✅ | | Free Trial Periods (Stripe) | ✅ | | Billing Portal (Stripe) | ✅ | | Webhooks for Stripe Events | ✅ | | Subscriptions & Payments API Routes | ✅ | | User Authentication (Supabase) | ✅ | | E-Mail (Mailgun) | ✅ | | Personalized Dashboard | ✅ | | Responsive Design + Landing Page | ✅ | | Logs & Monitoring (Datadog) | ✅ | You can learn more about the other features by visiting the following documentation page: [Sassy Documentation](https://github.com/marcelodosreis/sassy/blob/develop/docs). We are constantly improving Sassy with new features to make it even more powerful. You can find the current roadmap and planned features on our [Feature Roadmap](https://github.com/marcelodosreis/sassy/blob/develop/docs/feature-roadmap.md) ## Architecture and Structure Sassy's architecture is designed to streamline the rapid development of Micro-SaaS applications by providing essential features like user authentication, subscription management, and seamless payment processing. The project structure is clean and organized to help developers get started quickly while maintaining flexibility and scalability. ### Project Structure: ```bash src/ ├── app/ # Main logic and core functionality of the application ├── components/ # Reusable UI components ├── constants/ # Global constants and configurations ├── contexts/ # React contexts for global state management ├── hooks/ # Custom React hooks ├── libs/ # Third-party libraries and utilities ├── pages/ # Next.js pages corresponding to routes │ └── api/ # API routes for backend functionality ├── services/ # External API integrations and services ├── styles/ # TailwindCSS configuration and custom styles ├── utils/ # Utility functions and helpers └── middleware.ts # Middleware for request processing ``` ### Integration with Supabase and Stripe: - **Supabase** is used for user authentication and real-time database management. The `subscriptions` table is created to store subscription-related data for each user. - **Stripe** is integrated to handle payment processing and subscription plan management. ### SQL Script for Creating the `subscriptions` Table in Supabase: ```sql CREATE TABLE subscriptions ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v4(), user_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES auth.users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, stripe_subscription_id TEXT UNIQUE, plan TEXT CHECK (plan IN ('free', 'starter', 'creator', 'pro')) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'free', status TEXT CHECK (status IN ('active', 'canceled', 'past_due', 'incomplete', 'trialing')) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active', current_period_start TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, current_period_end TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE, created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW() ); ``` > **Note:** Since subscription data is sensitive, ensure that **Row Level Security (RLS)** is disabled for the `subscriptions` table. ### Environment Configuration: The environment variables are configured to integrate Sassy with Supabase and Stripe. Make sure to update the values accordingly. ```env NEXT_PUBLIC_PROJECT_URL= NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY= NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL= NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY= NEXT_PUBLIC_DATADOG_APPLICATION_ID= NEXT_PUBLIC_DATADOG_CLIENT_TOKEN= SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY= STRIPE_SECRET_KEY= STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET= DATADOG_SECRET_KEY= MAILGUN_SECRET_KEY= MAILGUN_SECRET_DOMAIN= ``` > **Note:** Replace the above values with your own Supabase and Stripe keys. ## Key Features - **Authentication with Supabase:** Utilize Supabase for user authentication, providing a secure and scalable login system. - **Subscription Management with Stripe:** Easily manage different subscription plans, handle payments, and track user subscriptions with Stripe integration. - **Responsive Design with TailwindCSS:** The application uses TailwindCSS for styling, ensuring a modern and responsive design out of the box. - **Built-in API Routes:** Ready-to-use API routes for managing subscriptions, payments, and user data. - **OAuth Support:** The app supports OAuth login via **Google**, **Facebook**, and **Twitter**, providing users with a seamless authentication experience. --- ## Webhook Listener for Stripe To handle incoming webhooks from Stripe (such as subscription updates, payment failures, etc.), Sassy includes a script for listening to Stripe webhooks: ```bash pnpm stripe:listen ``` This script connects your local environment to Stripe and listens for events like **invoice.payment_succeeded**, **invoice.payment_failed**, and more. It will automatically trigger the corresponding handler in your application to process the events. > **Note:** When using this in your development environment, make sure you have the Stripe secret key and webhook secret configured in your `.env.local` file. --- ## OAuth Authentication Sassy comes with built-in OAuth authentication support for popular platforms such as **Google**, **Facebook**, and **Twitter**. The authentication flow is fully integrated with Supabase, ensuring a secure and seamless experience for users. ### Dependencies: - OAuth SDKs for Google, Facebook, and Twitter to provide login functionality. With **OAuth**, users can authenticate with their preferred social media accounts, reducing friction in the signup/login process. OAuth tokens are securely managed by Supabase, and user data is synchronized across both Supabase and your application. > **Note:** The OAuth login functionality is already set up and fully supported out of the box. If you're using different authentication providers, you can easily extend this functionality by following the Supabase OAuth documentation. --- ## Setup Instructions ### 1. Install Dependencies Ensure that you have **pnpm** installed. If not, install it globally: ```bash npm install -g pnpm ``` Then, install the project dependencies: ```bash pnpm install ``` ### 2. Set Up Environment Variables Create a `.env.local` file in the root directory of the project and add the necessary environment variables (as provided in the **Environment Configuration** section). ### 3. Run the Development Server Once the environment is set up, start the development server: ```bash pnpm dev ``` The application will be available at `http://localhost:3000`. ### 4. Database Configuration To set up your Supabase project, run the provided SQL script to create the `subscriptions` table in your Supabase database. ### 5. Stripe Integration Make sure your Stripe API keys are correctly set up. You can test the payment processing using Stripe’s test keys in a sandbox environment. --- ## Development vs Production Environments For **development** and **production**, Sassy uses separate Supabase projects to ensure a clean and isolated environment. This allows you to safely test changes in the development environment without affecting live data in production. > **Note:** Ensure that you configure your `.env.local` with the correct Supabase project URL and keys for each environment. --- ## Conclusion Sassy provides a solid foundation for developing subscription-based Micro-SaaS applications. By leveraging the power of **Next.js**, **Supabase**, **Stripe**, **OAuth**, and **TailwindCSS**, you can rapidly build and deploy secure and scalable applications. Whether you're just starting a new SaaS product or iterating on an existing idea, Sassy makes it easy to focus on what matters most: delivering value to your users. --- For more information on integrating **Stripe**, **Supabase**, and **OAuth**, refer to the official documentation: - [Stripe Documentation](https://stripe.com/docs) - [Supabase Documentation](https://supabase.com/docs) - [OAuth Integration Guide](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/auth-helpers/oauth) - [Sassy Integration with Datadog](https://github.com/marcelodosreis/sassy/blob/main/docs/datadog.md)

Detailed tutorial: [docs/tutorial.md](docs/tutorial.md) | Full guide: [docs/guide.md](docs/guide.md) --- ## Manual Quick Start ```bash # 1. Clone & install git clone https://github.com/s87343472/backlink-pilot.git cd backlink-pilot && npm install # 2. Install bb-browser (recommended) npm install -g bb-browser # 3. Configure cp config.example.yaml config.yaml # Edit config.yaml with your product info # 4. Submit node src/cli.js submit futuretools --engine bb node src/cli.js submit https://any-site.com --engine bb ``` --- ## Engine Comparison | Engine | Setup | Pros | Cons | |--------|-------|------|------| | **bb-browser** (recommended) | `npm i -g bb-browser` | Real Chrome, invisible, OAuth works | Requires Chrome | | **playwright** (default) | `npm install` | No extra setup | Detected by anti-bot, blocked by Cloudflare | --- ## Commands ```bash node src/cli.js submit # Submit to directory node src/cli.js scout --deep # Discover form fields node src/cli.js awesome # Generate awesome-list Issue node src/cli.js indexnow # Ping search engines node src/cli.js status # Check submission history node src/cli.js bb-update # Update bb-browser adapters node src/batch-submit.js --limit N # Batch blog comments ``` --- ## Strategy **Why backlinks?** Google ranking = other sites linking to you = votes. More quality votes = higher ranking. ### Best channels by ROI 1. **GitHub awesome-lists** — highest ROI, permanent, $0, 5 min each 2. **Free directory sites** — 259 targets in `targets.yaml`, most auto-submittable 3. **Blog comments** — Website field backlinks, batch-automated ### Submission pace - 1-3 min between sites, 5-10 per day - **Never submit the same product to the same site twice** ### Sites to avoid | Site | Why | |------|-----| | IndieHub | Hidden $4.9 paywall | | OpenHunts | 51-week free queue | | toolify.ai | $99 | | Product Hunt | Anti-bot, manual only | --- ## Agent Integration ### Claude Code Clone the repo, run `claude`, and talk. `CLAUDE.md` is the instruction manual — Claude reads it automatically. ### OpenClaw ```bash ln -s ~/path/to/backlink-pilot ~/.openclaw/skills/backlink-pilot ``` Then just say: "Submit to free directories" --- ## # 🌻 Dandi API - Boilerplate for AI Micro SaaS Applications

**🤯 🤯 This repo was buikt with ENGLISH as the programming language with Cursor IDE and v0.🤯**


![Logo](https://github.com/emarco177/dandi/blob/main/public/demo.gif)

Dandi API is a comprehensive boilerplate repository for building AI-powered micro SaaS applications. It provides a solid foundation with essential components and functionalities needed to run an end-to-end micro SaaS application.

The service itself offers powerful insights, summaries, and analytics for open source GitHub repositories.

**🌐 Live Application: [https://www.dandi.cloud/](https://www.dandi.cloud/)**



## 🚀 Key Features

- **Complete Micro SaaS Structure**: Implements all necessary components for a fully functional AI micro SaaS application.
- **API Key Management**: Built-in system for handling API keys, UI heavily inspired by [Tavily](https://www.tavily.com/).
- **Rate Limiting**: Integrated rate limiting for API protection.
- **SSO Login**: Implemented Single Sign-On functionality.
- **AI Integration**: Leverages LangChain JS for AI capabilities.

## 🛠️ Built with Cursor IDE and v0

This entire project was developed using [Cursor IDE](https://cursor.com/), primarily through prompting with Cursor Composer and [v0](https://v0.dev/) . As a developer without frontend or full-stack experience, this project demonstrates the power of AI-assisted development.

**ENGLISH IS THE NEW PROGRAMMING LANGUAGE.**
[![udemy](https://img.shields.io/badge/Cursor%20Udemy%20Course-%20Coupon%20%2412.99-brightgreen)](https://www.udemy.com/course/cursor-ai-ide/?couponCode=APRIL-2026)

## 🧰 Tech Stack (TBH, Cursor did it all for me)

- **Frontend**: React, Next.js 13 (App Router), Tailwind CSS
- **Backend**: Node.js, Next.js API Routes
- **Database**: Supabase (PostgreSQL)
- **Authentication**: NextAuth.js
- **UI Components**: Shadcn UI, Radix UI
- **API**: RESTful API with rate limiting and API key authentication
- **AI**: LangChain JS 🦜🔗
- **Deployment**: Vercel 



## 🚀 Getting Started

To run this project locally, follow these steps:

1. Clone the repository:
   ```
   git clone https://github.com/emarco177/dandi.git
   cd dandi
   ```

2. Install dependencies:
   ```
   yarn install
   ```

3. Set up environment variables:
   Create a `.env.local` file in the root directory and add the necessary environment variables (refer to the Environment Variables section below).

4. Run the development server:
   ```
   yarn dev
   ```

5. Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000) in your browser to see the application.

## 🔐 Environment Variables

Create a `.env.local` file in the root directory with the following variables:

```
DB_URL=
DB_NAME=
DB_USER=
DB_PASSWORD=
GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=
GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=
NEXTAUTH_SECRET=
NEXTAUTH_URL=
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=
```

Note: Keep your `.env.local` file secure and never commit it to version control.

## 🏗️ Build and Production

To build the project for production:

```
yarn build
```

To run the production build locally:

```
yarn start
```

***S**imple **I**nventory **M**anagement and **P**roduct **L**ogistics* ![image](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=view&id=1WliiC62IAnbRIjaCLDmnzPm820IfNJJl) ## **Mockups**
## **Overall Summary**

SIMPL is a micro-SaaS application that is designed to improve the efficiency and maintainability of small and medium-sized businesses’ inventory and asset management capabilities. SIMPL does this by harnessing the power of Material UI, the Google Dart codebase, the Google Flutter framework, and the Google Firebase real-time database solution to provide a streamlined, simplistic, and elegant approach to inventory management and product logistics. Some primary use cases in which SIMPL excels is verifying and storing employee information, sharing databases between employees using invite-only security measures, generating QR codes for easy item tagging and tracking, scanning an item’s QR code to perform basic inventory tasks such as viewing item details, incrementing or decrementing item quantity, and building inventory reconciliation sheets. SIMPL also generates charts tracking item quantity over time, as well as store sales, so that users can make informed decisions about which products are high performers and which products simply cut into profit margins. Furthermore, SIMPL supports importing and exporting inventory data in CSV file format for further data manipulation in popular applications such as Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets.

## **What is the problem?**

In many small and medium-sized companies, inventory management is a burdensome and tedious task. Because of their size, many of these companies are unable to afford many of the more prominent inventory management applications, like Cin7 and Zoho. Furthermore, they have no need for many of the features that these applications provide, such as ecommerce integration, aftership tracking, serial number tracking, etc. These business owners simply need a way to keep track of what is in stock, what isn’t, and which items are providing the most profit. I saw this first-hand at the company I interned with in Summer 2021. Inventory reconciliation was being done by hand with paper every day. Employees would physically count the items on the shelves and mark the totals on paper to compare with what the online inventory was showing. When I asked the store supervisor about the reasoning behind hand-counting inventory, she said that she was unable to find a suitable software solution. As I began to research this issue further, trying to see if I could find a software alternative, I also started reading articles about how the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic had many reconsidering their job prospects, and how this was spurring the Great Resignation, which has led to an outgrowth of entrepreneurship and the creation of many small businesses. According to the Census Bureau, more than 4.4 million new businesses were created in the U.S. during 2020 alone. Pulling inspiration from my conversation with my supervisor, and the research I had done around inventory management software solutions, I saw a niche market and the idea of SIMPL was born. This new market of fledgling business owners and entrepreneurs has untapped potential in the realm of inventory management software, and SIMPL aims to be the answer.

## **How does SIMPL solve it?**

SIMPL will provide a service that many small and medium-sized business owners will benefit greatly from, without having to rely on any outside partnerships or external relationships. Using QR code technology in conjunction with the SIMPL app on iPhones, Androids, or Web-based devices, businesses will be able to manage their inventory in a quick and cost-efficient manner. Because SIMPL is cross-platform, it will be able to quickly integrate into a company’s workflow regardless of whether they use Apple, Android, or the Web-based devices. Also, because of CSV export capabilities, inventory data obtained through SIMPL can be shared and further analyzed through other applications if the user chooses to do so. This makes SIMPL a great addon for businesses that already have some form of inventory management in place, while also providing a competitive alternative for those who are in the market for a completely new system. SIMPL was built predominantly for phones, because we wanted to provide a cost-efficient solution for companies that didn’t want to invest in barcode scanner hardware and software. Utilizing QR code technology, as opposed to conventional barcodes, information retention capacity is greatly increased, being that a QR code has up to up to a 30% error correction capability. This means that up to 30% of the QR code can be damaged, by fading, dirt, accidental marking, scuffs, etc. and SIMPL can still read the information stored in the code. As inventory is moved between locations and endures the wear and tear of retail, this will reduce the headache that comes with inventory becoming unscannable due to damage to the barcode. Additionally, due to the more compact form of QR codes, printing costs may be decreased by up to 25% in certain use cases. Concerning logistics, SIMPL is designed to simplify communication first and foremost. Users will be able to see who last interacted with any item currently in the database. They will also be able to quickly and easily share stores with other users. Along with customary item insertion and deletion, SIMPL is designed to store scan-in and scan-out data for each item, allowing the application to generate detailed graphs concerning item quantity over a period of hours, days, months, or a year. For each store, SIMPL will also highlight which items are low in stock and which items are most popular, which will aid the user in making informed decisions about what items to purchase in the future. SIMPL also features an inventory reconciliation scan option, which will allow the user to scan the product on the physical store shelves, export that data to a separate CSV, and then compare the Official Inventory CSV to the Inventory Reconciliation CSV in order to find discrepancies quickly.

## **Who is the Target Market?**

Right now, our target market includes small to medium-sized retail companies, employing anywhere from 1 employee to 1000 employees, that either do not have an inventory management system in place, or would like to integrate a lightweight, cost-efficient addition into their current inventory management processes. With smaller businesses especially, there is a need to keep costs low. In doing so, more money can be put back into the business in the form of inventory and advertising, allowing the business to expand its profit margin and market presence. SIMPL is a solution for businesses who need inventory management and product logistics on a budget. As businesses reach those higher profit margins and bigger customer bases, inventory management becomes increasingly more important. Built with this in mind, SIMPL helps businesses establish a baseline for good inventory management practices early on, without divesting key funding that should be going to promote the business’s overall growth. We think that this affordability factor will be the main draw for customers who want to purchase and use the SIMPL software. Also, because of SIMPL’s availability on the major technology platforms (Web, Android, and iOS) we aim to be compatible with most, if not all, of the devices currently in use in our target market. Beyond our primary customer segment in retail , we would eventually like to bring SIMPL to small manufacturing companies and build a material requirement planning feature into the app, but that will depend on future development.

## **What is SIMPL's competitive advantage?**

There are a few other inventory management apps currently in the market, but, to our knowledge, none provide cross-platform support, an updated UI built to Google Material UI standards, an inventory reconciliation feature, and other streamlined features built specific to small and medium-sized businesses at a competitive price point. Many full-fledged software solutions and competitors, like Cin7, Ordoro, and Webgility, suffer from feature bloat and contain many tools that starting entrepreneurs and business owners may not need. SIMPL challenges the assumption that all of these extra features are necessary for an efficient management solution. Our research showed that features that generated Bill of Materials, Manufacturing Orders, or Purchase Orders, or integrated Point of Sale systems, were often under-utilized by many smaller business customers. Many of these bigger software options also lacked mobile apps to serve in the place of scanning hardware. Concerning the lightweight app sphere, we found that current apps such as Sortly, TookStock, and Telesto were very uniform in function, and there was not much to differentiate between them. None of these apps allowed users to see change in quantity over time graphically. Sortly was the only application that allowed QR code scanning, while TookStock was the only app that offered a semblance of inventory reconciliation. SIMPL provides these niche features while also covering the standard basics of item cataloging, item insertion/deletion, store insertion/deletion, and store share features. There seems to be an assumption that these are the only features necessary for smaller business owners. However, the entrepreneurial spirit continues to expand as COVID-19 restrictions lift and people become increasingly more independent, and they are looking for smarter and better ways to work. These future innovators and business creators need a way to manage their inventory without getting bogged down in feature bloat while still being able to integrate newer inventory technologies like QR codes, and see data in a visual way with graphs and charts. Current options in the app market don’t provide all of these features in one package, and SIMPL can fill in that gap.

Strava-Tool ===========



> A personal side project with Strava API using Python. --- ### Motivation This project is my personal side project with Strava API. The goal of this project is to analyze my training data for better future performance, as well as to **hone my Data Analysis & Visualization skills**. The idea was originally coming from the fact that my increasing demands for uploading indoor cycling activity data to Strava, especially in the lockdown time of COVID-19. I usually did indoor training with Zwift during the weekdays and long weekend group ride on the weekend. When training indoors with Zwift, I used to also record my cycling workout with a bicycle computer, for more workout information like power zone, laps, time, etc. This means there will be two generated files pointing to the same activity in the end. If you have authorized Zwift to connect with Strava beforehand, each of your virtual ride data will be AUTOMATICALLY synchronized to Strava. That's really exciting and satisfying when you saw a Strava notification telling you that "Your activity is ready." after suffering on the saddle for hours. (You know that feeling.😉) However, as an engineering graduate student and bike🚴 enthusiast, I decided to to take more control over the whole interaction process with Strava, in order to know what's happening under the hood. Therefore, I disabled the connection between the two Apps, and started developing a toy StravaAutoUploader tool with Python as the starting point of this side project. Hopefully it could be someday extended to have some advanced features like Golden Cheetah, TrainingPeaks, for analyzing, tracking, and predicting my performance on the bike!
